meta.title: Who really said "Life's most persistent and urgent question is, 'What are you doing for others?'"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: Genuinely King — but not from the 1957 sermon everyone cites. Quote Investigator traced it to Strength to Love (Harper & Row, 1963), page 72.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'Life's most persistent and urgent question is, 'What are you doing for others?''?
meta.ogDescription: Real King, wrong source. The line is printed in Strength to Love (1963), not in the 1957 sermon “Conquering Self-Centeredness” that gets credited.

answer.label: Written by
answer.sourceLine: The sentence closes a passage in King’s sermon “Three Dimensions of a Complete Life,” printed in his 1963 collection Strength to Love (Harper & Row, New York). Quote Investigator ↗ located it there and verified it on paper — the sermon starting at page 67, the quotation at page 72. What is not right is the source line the internet attaches to it: this is not from the 1957 sermon “Conquering Self-Centeredness.”
answer.confidenceText: Verified in print — but check the date before you cite it.

source.heading: Where it actually appears

docMeta.dd: 1963 · Harper & Row, New York (146 pp.) · quotation at page 72

source.excerpt: Light has come into the world, and every man must decide whether he will walk in the light of creative altruism or the darkness of destructive selfishness. This is the judgment. Life’s most persistent and urgent question is, ‘What are you doing for others?’
trail: Quote Investigator ↗ concludes the quotation appeared in a collection of sermons and essays authored by King in 1963, citing Strength to Love, sermon “Three Dimensions of a Complete Life,” start page 67, quote page 72, Harper & Row, New York — and marks that citation “Verified on paper.”

Stanford’s Online King Records Access record ↗ for Strength to Love lists it as a 146-page book published New York: Harper & Row, 1963, and names “Three Dimensions of a Complete Life” among its contents.

The King Institute’s full transcript of “Conquering Self-Centeredness” ↗ — Dexter Avenue Baptist Church, 11 August 1957, taken from an audio recording of the service — contains no such sentence, though that sermon is the source most often named for it.

Quote Investigator’s chronology continues past the book: the same sermon and passage were reprinted in A Martin Luther King Treasury (1964), and The Ottawa Journal of 31 December 1968 described an Anglican primate’s Christmas card carrying the quotation credited to King — both documented on the QI page ↗.
source.excerptNote: The passage as printed in Strength to Love and reproduced by Quote Investigator ↗, which cites the sermon at start page 67 and the quotation at page 72.

sourceLink.text: Stanford King Institute catalogue record for Strength to Love

source.rightsHolder: The Estate of Martin Luther King, Jr., Inc. (licensed through Intellectual Properties Management); originally published by Harper & Row
source.rightsNote: Strength to Love was first published in 1963, so it is firmly in copyright in the United States. Stanford’s King Institute states plainly that it cannot give permission to reproduce King’s writings and directs requests to Intellectual Properties Management, the exclusive licensor of the King estate ↗. Quoting the sentence for attribution and commentary is ordinary fair use; reprinting the sermon is not.

author.name: Martin Luther King Jr.
author.heading: About Martin Luther King Jr.
author.metaLine: 1929–1968 · Baptist minister and leader of the American civil rights movement
author.bio: Martin Luther King Jr. was a Baptist minister and the foremost leader of the American civil rights movement, whose nonviolent resistance was grounded in Christian agape love. He pastored Dexter Avenue Baptist Church in Montgomery — where he preached the 1957 sermon so often misidentified as this quotation’s source — before returning to Atlanta as co-pastor of Ebenezer. Strength to Love (1963), the sermon collection in which this line was published, was drafted in part during a fifteen-day jail stay in Albany, Georgia, and became the first volume of sermons by an African American preacher widely available to a white readership.

cite.sourceCitation: Martin Luther King Jr., “Three Dimensions of a Complete Life,” in Strength to Love (New York: Harper & Row, 1963), 72. The sermon begins at page 67; the page was verified on paper by Quote Investigator, “Quote Origin: Life’s Most Persistent and Urgent Question Is, ‘What Are You Doing for Others?’” (18 January 2016). The commonly cited 1957 sermon “Conquering Self-Centeredness” does not contain the sentence.

misattribution.heading: The author is right. The citation usually isn’t.
misattribution.intro: This is one of the rare cases where a famous name attached to a feel-good line is actually correct — and the error has migrated into the footnote instead. Almost every version you will meet online pins the sentence to a sermon that does not contain it.

items.who: “Conquering Self-Centeredness,” Dexter Avenue Baptist Church, 11 August 1957
items.why: This is the citation attached to the quotation almost everywhere. The King Institute publishes the complete text of that sermon ↗, transcribed from an audio recording of the service, and neither “persistent and urgent” nor “doing for others” appears anywhere in it. The sermon genuinely is about self-centredness and service — which is presumably why the pairing felt right to whoever first made it.

Wikiquote does carry the sentence, but reading the page carefully matters: it sits under the heading “Conquering Self-centeredness (1957) ↗” as a listed variant, sourced not to the sermon but to The Words of Martin Luther King, Jr. by Coretta Scott King, Second Edition (2011), chapter “Community of Man,” p. 3. The variant text printed there is a blend — the 1957 sermon’s opening spliced onto the “creative altruism … destructive selfishness” passage that belongs to the 1963 book.

BrainyQuote ↗ and PassItOn ↗ both print the wording exactly and both give no speech, book or date whatsoever — only King’s name. A sentence circulating without a citation is a sentence that will eventually acquire one, correctly or not.

In January 2015 the Jim Crow Museum at Ferris State University published the result of a genuine hunt for the source: “the most common attribution is to Dr. King’s 1957 speech, Conquering Self-Centeredness. But the quote is not there … this quote cannot be authenticated as being attributed to Dr. King” (Question of the Month, January 2015 ↗). That was the right call on the evidence then to hand, and the museum explicitly allowed that a record might yet surface. One did.

items.who: The sermon King preached under this title
items.why: King delivered “The Three Dimensions of a Complete Life” many times. The two full transcripts published by the King Institute that we read — the Dexter Avenue version ↗ and the Friendship Baptist Church version ↗ — do not contain this sentence. That is a note about those two transcripts, not proof he never said it aloud; the documented wording is the printed one.

misattribution.truthLine: It really is King. Quote Investigator ↗ found the exact wording on the printed page — Strength to Love, Harper & Row, 1963, in the sermon “Three Dimensions of a Complete Life,” page 72. Cite the book, not the 1957 sermon.

context.heading: A sermon that only became this sentence in print
lead: Strength to Love was assembled under difficult conditions. The King Institute records that King proposed a sermon collection to Harper in early 1957 but had produced nothing by mid-1962; he finally drafted several of the sermons during fifteen days in an Albany, Georgia jail cell in July 1962 ↗, and finished the volume while preparing for the Birmingham campaign in early 1963.

Editing changed the book. The King Institute notes that editors Melvin Arnold and Charles Wallis struck a good deal of King’s sharper language — his description of segregation as one of “the ugly practices of our nation,” his call for “a deep-seated change” in capitalism, much of his anti-war writing. What survived was the preaching a white readership could receive, and it made Strength to Love the first volume of sermons by an African American preacher widely available to that audience. This sentence is a product of that printed, edited form rather than of any one Sunday morning.
context.detailsSummary: King’s own misgivings about sermons on the page
detailsBody: King was uneasy about the translation from pulpit to page. In the book’s preface he wrote that his reservations had “grown out of the fact that a sermon is not an essay to be read but a discourse to be heard,” and conceded as the book went to press that he had “not altogether overcome my misgivings” — both lines quoted in the King Institute’s entry on the book ↗.
The irony is worth sitting with. The sentence that has become one of King’s most reproduced calls to service is a written one — and the mis-citation habit keeps handing it back to the pulpit.
context.pull: a sermon is not an essay to be read but a discourse to be heard
